items.title: Add salt
items.because: Salt is 2,372 ppm, below the 2800-3200 ppm the cell needs. A cell run under its salt band makes less chlorine and wears out faster.
items.why: Salt is 2,372 ppm against a 2,800 to 3,200 band, so the cell has less to work with and makes less chlorine, and it wears out faster running under its band. Adding this dose should raise salt by about 628 ppm.
items.how: Run the pump the whole time, and stand at the shallow end or by the skimmer so you can reach the water. Scoop the 90 lb into a 5-gallon bucket of pool water in batches, stir until it dissolves, and pour it slowly around the deep end. Never dump dry salt on the liner, because undissolved granules sitting on vinyl can bleach and weaken it.

dose.label: 90 lb of salt (about 2.25 of a 40 lb bag)

items.title: Empty the skimmer basket
items.because: Last emptied 3 days ago; the cadence is every 3.
items.why: You last emptied it 3 days ago and the cadence is every 3. A full basket restricts flow to the pump and the cell, and the cell only makes chlorine from water moving through it.
items.how: Leave the pump running, lift the skimmer lid and pull the basket. Dump the debris away from the pool, rinse the basket, and set it back in firmly. Empty it before you add the salt so flow is at its best when the dose circulates.

items.title: Leave the cell alone for now
items.because: ORP is 588 mV, under the at least 600 mV floor -- but Salt is out of band too, and ORP sits downstream of all of it. Fix that first, give the water a full day to circulate, then re-read. Turning the cell up now just means running it harder against the same problem.
items.why: ORP is 588 mV against a floor of at least 600 mV, but salt is also out of band, and ORP depends on the chlorine the cell can make from that salt. Turning the cell up now would just run it harder against the same problem.
items.how: Do nothing to the cell today. Once the salt has had a full day to circulate, take a fresh reading and judge ORP then. Keep the pump running so the new salt mixes through the water.

items.title: The cell is already flat out
items.because: The cell is at 100% (from config.json), running 24 hours a day, so there is no headroom left to ask for -- this is not a setting you can turn up. Salt is out of band, and each of those starves the cell in its own way: low salt gives it less to work with, high pH wastes the chlorine it makes, low CYA lets the sun burn it off. Fix those and the same cell will produce more.
items.why: The cell is already at 100% and running 24 hours a day, so there is no headroom to turn it up. Low salt at 2,372 ppm gives it less to work with, and pH at 7.78 sits at the top of its band, so fixing salt is what lets the same cell produce more. CYA was not measured, so I can say nothing about how well the chlorine is being protected from the sun.
items.how: There is nothing to adjust here, and the cell stays at 100%. Leave the setting alone and let the salt dose do the work. Check the cell output again after tomorrow's reading.

items.title: Leave the pump schedule alone for now
items.because: The pump is running 24 hours a day, which is a lot -- but on a saltwater pool the pump schedule is the chlorine schedule, because the cell only makes chlorine while water is going through it. With ORP at 588 mV, cutting hours would cut production exactly when you need it. Get ORP comfortably over 600 with the cell below full, and that is the moment to start trimming hours and watching what happens.
items.why: The pump runs 24 hours a day, which is a lot, but on a saltwater pool the cell only makes chlorine while water is moving through it. With ORP at 588 mV, cutting hours now would cut chlorine production when you need it.
items.how: Leave the timer exactly as it is. Once ORP is comfortably over 600 with the cell below full, that is the time to start trimming hours. The pump also needs to keep running through today's salt dose so it disperses evenly.

items.title: Test borates
items.because: Borates aren't on the ICO panel and haven't been tested. The target is 50 ppm; a strip test once a season is enough to know where you are.
items.why: Borates have never been measured, since they are not on the ICO panel, and the target is 50 ppm. A strip test once a season tells you where you stand.
items.how: Dip a borate strip or use a test kit on a water sample taken from elbow depth, away from the return. Follow the timing on the package and write the number down. Log the result so it shows up as a measured value next time.

safety_rules: NEVER pour undiluted acid into the skimmer. Acid down the skimmer runs neat through the pump, heater and salt cell and eats them. Dilute it and pour it slowly around the deep end with the pump running.

NEVER put shock and acid in the same session without at least 4 hours between them, and say the gap out loud in the instructions. Both move pH hard in opposite directions, and back to back you cannot tell what the water actually did.
ALWAYS predissolve dry chemicals in a 5-gallon bucket of pool water before they go in. Undissolved granules sitting on a vinyl liner bleach and weaken it.
NEVER put chlorine and acid in the same bucket, in either order. That combination produces chlorine gas.
ALWAYS add acid to water, never water to acid -- pouring water into acid can boil and spit it back at you.
The pump must be RUNNING before anything goes in, and keep running afterwards, so a dose disperses instead of sitting in one corner.
headline: Salt is low at 2,372 ppm; add salt today and leave the cell and pump alone
summary: The reading is from this morning. Salt is well under its band, and ORP is at 588 mV against a 600 floor, which follows from the low salt. pH is 7.78, inside its band. Add the salt first, keep everything else as is, and re-read tomorrow. CYA, TA, CH and free chlorine were not measured.
